Task Force Iron Gate is intended to stop armaments, missile and drone parts, entering the Islamic Republic from Pakistan, Iraq and Central Asia among others
A surface-to-air missile system displayed at an exhibition of missiles and drones at the National Aerospace Park outside Tehran on 12 November 2026 (AFP)
On
The US has stepped up its efforts to choke Iran’s military supplies with the announcement of Task Force Iron Gate, a new unit aimed at blocking imports of weapons entering the Islamic Republic overland and via the Caspian Sea.
Washington and Tehran are locked in negotiations to end the current war, which has now lasted over eight months, crashed global markets, and has no clear end in sight.
While Iran produces the bulk of its weapons domestically, it has looked increasingly towards military imports from the north, amid the ongoing US naval blockade of its southern ports, which has brought its usual maritime trade routes to a near-standstill.
Arms and their components have entered Iran through Russia and Central Asia, while there is also growing evidence of sales from China.
Deliveries of the parts used in Iran’s home-produced missiles and drones have also been traced to manufacturers in countries opposed to the Islamic Republic, including the US itself.
Operational details are scarce about how the 20-person unit, inaugurated by US Admiral Brad Cooper of US Central Command in Tampa, Florida, will operate.
The task force also seeks to further block Iranian exports, the most lucrative being oil, which Washington has sanctioned and blockaded in its bid to curb what it calls Iran's "illegal revenue streams".

The British government has unveiled its first set of sanctions against Israeli companies linked to illegal West Bank settlements, after announcing comprehensive sanctions in September.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the sanctions on Tuesday, shortly before tenders for the E1 settlement bloc - which would effectively split the occupied West Bank in two - are scheduled to be allocated by the Israeli government.
The sanctions are targeting eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural business firms.
The UK is also sanctioning Tsav9, an Israeli group involved in stopping aid trucks from entering Gaza, which the United States also sanctioned in 2024.
The Foreign Office described Tsaz9 as "an Israeli activist movement whose stated mission has been to stop humanitarian aid entering the Gaza Strip, and which has organised and carried out blockades of crossings, ports and roads used by humanitarian aid convoys bound for Gaza".
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."
The foreign secretary added: "And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable."

On
Early last month, the chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced the launch of Operation Fajr al-Yemen (Dawn of Yemen), aimed at restoring state institutions, retaking the capital, Sanaa, and ending Houthi control.
The announcement came a day after the Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, seized large areas of Taiz governorate and took control of all entrances to Taiz city.
However, no advances have been made on the ground since the operation was announced. Instead, the Houthis have continued to make major gains in both Taiz and Lahij governorates, in Yemen's southwest.
On the west coast, battles were ongoing in Dhubab district, where government forces controlled the Dhubab military airport and surrounding areas. Meanwhile, the Houthis were advancing through the mountains and valleys of Lahij governorate and were on the verge of imposing a siege on military forces along the coast.
On Sunday, 15 November, Yemeni government forces announced the withdrawal of their troops from the Bab al-Mandab area and Dhubab military airport as part of a redeployment aimed at securing the provisional capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates.
The Houthis advanced into all the areas previously held by government forces on the same day. They are now roughly 70km from Aden's northern entrance, while government forces are regrouping to defend the city.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq demands his release
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq demands his release
The family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq has demanded that his place of detention be disclosed and that he be released, following his arrest by the Israeli army at dawn on Sunday.
Israeli soldiers raided his home in the town of Burqin, west of Jenin, blew open the door, and searched the premises before taking Atiq to an unknown location. His family has yet to receive any information regarding his whereabouts or the conditions of his detention.
Atiq’s arrest comes amid an ongoing campaign of pursuit and detention targeting Palestinian journalists due to their professional work.
The Journalists' Syndicate has reported that approximately 210 journalists including about 23 women have been arrested since 7 October 2023. Meanwhile, the Palestinian Prisoners' Club confirms that 38 journalists, including five women, remain in Israeli occupation prisons.
Atiq works as a photojournalist for several international outlets, including Middle East Eye. About a month ago, he was detained for several hours while filming the olive harvest in the village of Anza, near Jenin.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Israeli settlers kill Palestinian grandmother in her home in Jericho
Israeli settlers shot dead an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded eight of her family members, including her children and grandchildren, during an attack on a home in the village of Ein al-Duyuk al-Tahta, west of Jericho in the occupied West Bank.
Eyewitnesses told Middle East Eye that armed settlers entered the Palestinian home in the middle of the night on Monday and shot 73-year-old Fidda Fheidat in the head, killing her on the spot.
The settlers, who had recently seized eight Palestinian homes in an area adjacent to the village, went on to fire at other members of the family, wounding eight of them.
Ahmad Fheidat, the victim’s brother-in-law, said that on hearing the gunfire, he rushed to repel the settlers.
He felt a sharp pain in his leg and realised he had been shot; looking behind him, he saw Fidda lying on the ground, bleeding from her head.
"Despite the injury, I rushed towards her and called out to her. When I placed my hand on her head, I saw that her skull had been split open by the close-range fire; her blood had splattered onto the walls of the house," he said.

Sixty-six British MPs from across the political spectrum have called on their government to use its veto as a permanent member of the UN Security Council to stop the UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh from becoming the world body's next secretary general.
In a letter to Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, Liberal Democrat MP Monica Harding writes that Nusseibeh is “not a credible candidate” for the role because she has "repeatedly denied and dismissed" reports by the UN Panel of Experts and other groups linking the UAE to the war in Sudan.
A recent confidential quarterly report from the UN Panel of Experts on Sudan, which was obtained by Middle East Eye, established conclusively that the UAE had hired Colombian mercenaries to fight for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudanese paramilitary group that the UN and US determined has committed genocide in Darfur.
The UAE has armed and equipped the RSF using supply lines that run through Libya, Chad, Ethiopia and the breakaway Somali regions of Puntland and Somaliland. Abu Dhabi continues to deny the charges.
Nusseibeh, an Emirati diplomat of Palestinian descent, is one of eight candidates seeking to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December.
MEE understands that the Security Council’s next straw poll - an informal, anonymous poll on whether members encourage, discourage or have no opinion about a candidate - will take place on Thursday.

Serbia’s election-winning Student List has pledged to halt arms trade with Israel and called for an end to an Israeli-linked drone project in Serbia, signalling a potential break with the close military ties that former President Aleksandar Vucic cultivated.
Filip Ubovic, a Student List representative, announced the pledge last week on a podcast hosted by British journalist Aaron Bastani.
“What is happening there is a stain on humanity’s conscience, and it is truly regrettable. Our platform clearly states that we will end the arms trade with Israel,” said Ubovic when asked about Israel’s war on Gaza.
The Student List won 140 of 250 seats in the 25 October snap election, securing an outright majority and defeating Vucic’s bloc after years of accusations of growing authoritarianism and corruption under his rule.
In September, a month before the election, Vucic inaugurated a factory assembling Israeli-made drones in Serbia.
Serbian arms exports to Israel rose from $1.5m to $45.8m in 2024, according to a joint investigation by the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network and Haaretz. The surge coincided with Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Serbia also stepped up its purchases of Israeli weapons. In early 2025, it bought Elbit Systems’ PULS artillery systems and Hermes drones for $335m. In August that year, it bought long-range missiles, drones and electronic warfare equipment for about $1.6bn.

data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Crew abandon gas tanker off Hormuz after being hit by projectile, sources say
The crew of a liquefied petroleum gas tanker abandoned ship on Tuesday after the vessel was struck by a projectile while sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, maritime security sources said.
The crew of the Panama-flagged Tara Gas LPG tanker abandoned ship around 7 nautical miles (13 km) off Oman's Khasab coast, the sources said, and one crew member remains missing.
The vessel's Marshall Islands-based owner, listed in databases as Global Gas, could not be reached for comment.
The vessel last reported its position on September 26 off Oman's coast, according to ship tracking data on the MarineTraffic platform.
Earlier on Tuesday, British navy linked agency UKMTO said the crew of a tanker passing through the Strait of Hormuz was unaccounted for after it was attacked for a second time north of the port city of Khasab in Oman. It gave no further details.

Off
Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab died on Tuesday in Turkey at the age of 62. Fellow campaigners said he died after suffering a heart attack.
Ebrahim Sharif, an activist who was a close friend of the family, told the Associated Press that Rajab’s wife and daughter found him unresponsive early in the morning at their home in Turkey.
Reflecting on the activist's life, Sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, advocacy director at the London-based Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy, described him as a "beautiful soul" who was "as noble as his name [Nabeel]".
"Nabeel defended our rights with dignity and paid a heavy personal price, as did his family, for standing up for the rights of his people," Wadaei wrote on X.
"He suffered imprisonment and abuse by the state for exposing human rights violations. He left Bahrain after witnessing the body of Sayed Mohamed Almousawi, who was murdered under torture."
Rajab left Bahrain early in the Iran war and fled to Turkey after fearing he would be imprisoned again by Bahrain for releasing a statement accusing the government of the death of Almousawi, a former political prisoner.
Rajab, who became one of the most recognisable figures of the country’s pro-democracy movement, spent much of his adult life challenging the authorities over political repression, torture and restrictions on freedom of expression.

“There is no ceasefire in Gaza. People talk about a ceasefire but at best it’s a reduced fire,” Chris Sidoti said in the latest episode of the Expert Witness Podcast. “The killing continues on a daily basis, including the killing of children.”
“The circumstances that gave rise to our finding of genocide are still operative inside Gaza. And until those circumstances change fundamentally, then the genocidal activities of the Israeli authorities will continue,” the lawyer and expert on international human rights law said.
Sidoti is a former Australian human rights commissioner who also served on the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar.
His remarks follow two major reports by the UN's Palestine commission this year, including a report in June concluding that Israel had deliberately targeted children in Gaza, committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the coastal enclave, as well as further war crimes in the West Bank.
In October, the commission presented its fifth report to the UN General Assembly, finding again that Israel was committing genocidal acts in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
Both reports built on the commission’s finding in September 2025 that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to hold joint defence pact talks
Officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will hold their latest round of talks for their Mecca Joint Defence Pact later this month, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Tuesday.
In a news conference with his Syrian counterpart, Asaad al-Shibani, Fidan also said officials from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, Britain and Italy, as well as Turkey, would hold their second collective meeting in November.

Despite all her judicial problems, polls still suggest that National Rally leader Marine Le Pen will most likely win next year’s presidential election in France by a significant margin.
By instrumentalising massive popular discontent, economic hardships, xenophobia, and the scapegoating of non-western peoples and cultures, Le Pen has turned what used to be a fringe group into France’s largest political party.
She has capitalised on a devastated social landscape created by decades of neoliberal capitalist policies, successfully stealing the historical terrain and voters of the left and far left.
Today, no other party can compete with the National Rally. Only a large coalition could defeat her at the polls next April. It is thus very probable that France may soon be governed by the xenophobic, Islamophobic, ultra-nationalist far right.
But if Le Pen is made of titanium, accusations of antisemitism in her party may prove to be her kryptonite.
Jordan Bardella, her chosen heir and potential future prime minister, has denied writing antisemitic messages attributed to him in the mid-2010s, when he was a teenager. But the French outlet Mediapart says it was able to verify Bardella as the author, including by obtaining a judicially certified copy of the original 2013 messages from the US social media giant Meta.
So far, the accusations have not made a dent in the National Rally’s support. And in recent weeks, the controversy has been overshadowed by the high-school student protest movement that took France by storm in September.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
The UN migration agency has warned of further deaths from hypothermia in Gaza as Israel continues to heavily restrict the entry of shelter aid into the territory.
Heavy rains swept through the war-torn enclave last week, inundating thousands of makeshift tents where the majority of Gaza's population is sheltering. A nine-month-old baby died from the cold amid the plummeting temperatures.
"Without proper shelter, without critical relief items, then hypothermia deaths will occur," Karl Baker, head of the International Organization for Migration's Gaza programme, said on Tuesday, adding that children were particularly vulnerable, since they lose body heat more quickly. "It's unacceptable to have hypothermia in the modern world."
Baker said that some 100,000 tents were prepositioned outside Gaza, but the Israeli authorities had barred the entry of items which they consider to be "dual use"- predominantly shelter items including tent poles and mobile homes.
Baker described meeting a drenched family sheltering beneath sagging, worn-out tarpaulins. "Gaza is turning into one large IDP camp (internally displaced persons). It ranks as one of the worst I've walked through," he said.
Reporting by Reuters
